cells.verb: letting what was never true come down
cells.place: in the part of you that knows what matters before it can say why
cells.ask: give the one thing that stayed standing a little steady, unhurried attention each day, so the clearing keeps serving what matters instead of needing another collapse
cells.core:
When something in you gives way right now, it's because it was never holding. You can feel the difference between a wall that's load-bearing and one that was only painted to look like it — and the painted ones are coming down without you having to argue them down. It isn't wreckage. It's room.

What's free now is quieter work: a little steady, unhurried time each day with the one thing that stayed standing, kept up by attention rather than by anything dramatic. Not to fix it. To tend it. Clearing keeps its truth when something gets built in the space it opened.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what's really holding, and you let the rest go.

cells.tense: Future — bracing at a future that can't be written in.
cells.verb: tearing down whatever stands long enough to be seen
cells.place: in the part of you that knows what matters before it can say why
cells.ask: pick one thing other people handed you and keep it this week, exactly as they did it, before deciding whether it was false — so that what falls next falls because you saw through it, not because you got there first
cells.core:
You're knocking things down before they've had a chance to be false. Somewhere ahead is a cleaner version of your life with nothing untested left standing, and you're racing toward it — so every idea, habit, loyalty that shows up gets its legs kicked out as a matter of principle. It feels like clarity. It's starting to look like nothing can stay.

The knowing that matters here doesn't move that fast; it recognizes what to keep as surely as what to drop. One thing other people handed you — a practice, a saying, a way of doing something — kept this week exactly the way they did it, before you rule on it. Let something stand long enough to show you whether it holds. Then what falls will fall because you saw through it, not because you got there first.
cells.sheetLine: You're tearing things down faster than you can see them.

cells.tense: Past — still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: propping up what has already stopped holding
cells.place: in the part of you that knows what matters before it can say why
cells.ask: build one small thing that works right now — an order for the week, a plan, a place where things go — and let it carry real weight, so that what's been leaning on you has somewhere else to rest
cells.core:
You've known for a while that this doesn't hold anymore. You're still holding it up. The arrangement, the belief, the way things were supposed to work — it stopped doing its job some time back, and what you've been calling loyalty is mostly your own shoulder under a beam that isn't attached to anything.

The way through isn't to drop it; that door's already behind you and it won't be forced from this side. It's to make something that actually works. One small thing, built now — an order for your week, a plan, a place where things go — and let it bear real weight. When there's something sound to lean on, the dead thing gets lighter on its own, and you'll find you've set it down without deciding to.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding up something that already let go of you.

cells.tense: Disowned present — pen down in a room you're already writing.
cells.verb: letting what can't hold fall without seeing that you're the one who stopped holding it
cells.place: in the part of you that knows what matters before it can say why
cells.ask: move toward the one thing you actually want today, before checking whether the old reasons permit it — and notice what gives way when you do, because that's yours
cells.core:
Something in your life is coming apart, and you've been describing it as weather. Things keep not working the way they're supposed to; reasons that used to hold you have quietly gone slack. You call it bad luck, or timing, or other people. But you're the one who stopped believing in them, and some part of you knew what mattered before any of it started to slide.

The way back isn't to understand the collapse. It's simpler and earlier than that: move toward the one thing you actually want today, before you check whether the old reasons allow it. Then watch what gives way when you do. That's the part you've been calling circumstance. It's been yours the whole time.
cells.sheetLine: Things are falling, and you're calling it weather.

flags.detail: "for years" — a cell knows no one's past
